passage:
Monday: At the colony sandpit, Chinmay told Kiaan, “Arun is my best friend. You can't play with us.” Kiaan walked away slowly. Vishal, Chinmay's father, saw it.
Tuesday: At bedtime Vishal said, “You love Arun, and that's lovely. But how did Kiaan feel yesterday?” Chinmay thought. “Sad.” “Can best friends still play with other kids?” “…Maybe.”
Thursday: Chinmay called, “Kiaan! You can be the digger driver. Arun and me are the builders.” The three of them dug a tunnel together.

qa.q: What job did Chinmay give Kiaan on Thursday?
qa.a: Digger driver.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay tell Kiaan he couldn't play?
qa.a: He felt fond and loyal to Arun and wanted to keep him close, not realising it would hurt Kiaan.

qa.q: What did Vishal do that helped Chinmay include Kiaan?
qa.a: He praised Chinmay's love for Arun, then asked how Kiaan felt and whether best friends can play with others, so Chinmay found the answer himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Kiaan when he was told he couldn't play?
qa.a: He was hurt and left out, which is why he walked away slowly.

grounding: Over a week, a child learns that loyalty to a best friend doesn't mean excluding and hurting another child.

passage: Rain kept the whole class indoors, and there was only one small play kitchen. Vasudha stood in front of it with her friend Tia, arms out. “Only me and Tia. We're best friends.” A new girl, holding a toy pot, stepped back. Samir Sir came over. “You two love playing together. That's nice. Can best friends make room for a cook?” Vasudha frowned. “But then it's not just us.” “It can still be you two, plus one.” Tia whispered, “She can be the guest.” Vasudha shrugged. “Okay. Guest.”

qa.q: What was the new girl holding?
qa.a: A toy pot.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she frowned at Samir Sir's idea?
qa.a: She felt worried that letting someone in would spoil her closeness with Tia.

qa.q: How did Samir Sir help Vasudha see closeness differently?
qa.a: He praised the friendship and suggested it could still be the two of them plus one, so closeness could include others.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel when she's invited as the guest?
qa.a: She'd likely feel relieved and included after being shut out.

grounding: On a crowded indoor day, a child tries to keep her best friend to herself, and her teacher shows closeness can include others.

passage: In the colony lane, Asif hooked his arm round Ramesh's neck. “You're my best friend, so don't play with Kunal. Promise?” Ramesh looked at Kunal, who was holding a cricket bat and waiting. He didn't know what to say. Asif's Ammi, drying clothes on the balcony, called down. “Asif, being best friends is good. But telling Ramesh not to play with Kunal hurts Kunal. You can be best friends and still play together.” Asif pouted, then let go. “Okay. Kunal bats first.”

qa.q: What was Kunal holding?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when Asif asked him to promise?
qa.a: He was probably torn and uncomfortable, caught between his best friend and Kunal, who was waiting to play.

qa.q: What did Asif's Ammi teach about loyalty?
qa.a: That being best friends is good, but it shouldn't mean hurting someone else, and all three could play.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Asif's words?
qa.a: Kunal would feel left out and hurt, since he was being kept away on purpose.

grounding: A child tries to keep his best friend away from another boy, and his mother teaches that loyalty does not mean hurting someone else.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage:
“Papa, I love you a hundred thousand million!” Lalit threw his arms round Deepak's neck. “I'll never ever leave you, even when I'm big.”
“Never?”
“Never ever. I'll live in your room.”
Deepak laughed and hugged him. An hour later: “No ice cream before dinner.” Lalit stamped his foot. “I don't love you anymore!”
“Hmm. That's a big change,” said Deepak calmly.
At bedtime Lalit crept into his lap. “I love you again. A hundred thousand million.”
“I know,” said Deepak.

qa.q: Where did Lalit say he'd live when he's big?
qa.a: In Papa's room.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he said “I don't love you anymore!”?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated about the ice cream in that moment; it didn't mean his love had really gone.

qa.q: What did Deepak understand about Lalit's words, and how did he respond?
qa.a: He knew the words showed strong feelings of the moment, not fixed promises, so he stayed calm and warm.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when Lalit says “I love you again” at bedtime?
qa.a: He probably feels touched and amused, knowing the love was always there.

grounding: A preschooler's I love you and I don't love you show strong feelings in the moment, and his father takes them calmly.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage:
Creche note from Uma, day carer.
Today Yogesh gave me a drawing: a big yellow sun, two stick people holding hands, and “UMA” in wobbly letters. He said, “I love you, Uma Aunty. I love you more than Mummy.” I thanked him warmly and told him, “Your mummy is lucky to have your love too.” At pick-up, he ran to his mother shouting, “I love you most, Mummy!” Children his age say big words with big feeling. I'm keeping the drawing on my wall. 😊

qa.q: What did Yogesh draw?
qa.a: A big yellow sun, two stick people holding hands, and “UMA” in wobbly letters.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he gave Uma the drawing?
qa.a: He felt affection and warmth for Uma, and wanted to show it with a gift and big words.

qa.q: Why was Uma's reply wise?
qa.a: Uma thanked him warmly but gently reminded him that his mummy is lucky to have his love too, so his words didn't set up a rivalry.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She'd likely feel amused and reassured, knowing his big words are strong feelings of the moment.

grounding: The carer's note shows a preschooler saying I love you and giving a drawing, words that show strong feelings in the moment.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage: On the way to the village school, Hafsa picked a fistful of yellow wildflowers from the ditch. She gave them to Ankita Ma'am at the gate, stems dripping. “For you. I love you, Ma'am. When I'm big I'll marry you.” The other children giggled. Ankita crouched and took the flowers carefully. “Thank you, Hafsa. These are beautiful. I love teaching you.” She put them in a steel tumbler on her desk. Hafsa checked on them three times that morning.

qa.q: Where did Ankita Ma'am put the flowers?
qa.a: In a steel tumbler on her desk.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she gave the flowers?
qa.a: She felt deep affection for her teacher and wanted to show it with a gift and big words.

qa.q: How did Ankita Ma'am respond to Hafsa's big promise?
qa.a: She accepted the flowers warmly and said she loved teaching her, gently taking the feeling without the promise.

qa.q: How might the other children see Hafsa's big promise?
qa.a: They found it funny, which is why they giggled, while Ankita Ma'am took the feeling behind it seriously.

grounding: A child shows love with wildflowers and a big promise, and her teacher receives the feeling kindly.

passage:
Note by Manoj, KG teacher.
Charu has been admiring Mitali's drawings all week. “You draw so good!” she says, and copies Mitali's rainbows. Today I put Mitali's rainbow on the wall. Charu looked at it, then at her own, and said, “Yours is ugly.” Mitali's face fell. I took Charu aside. She said, “Mine isn't on the wall.” She felt left out. I told her how much I liked her purple sky, and asked if she'd say sorry to Mitali. She did, and put her own drawing up tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Charu copy from Mitali?
qa.a: Her rainbows.

qa.q: Why did Charu call Mitali's drawing ugly?
qa.a: She felt left out and jealous when Mitali's rainbow went on the wall and hers didn't, so her admiration flipped to rivalry.

qa.q: How did Manoj handle the flip from praise to rivalry?
qa.a: Manoj talked to Charu privately, found out she felt left out, praised her own work, and invited her to make up with Mitali.

qa.q: What was it like for Mitali when Charu called her drawing ugly?
qa.a: She was hurt, since Charu had praised her drawings all week.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler's honest praise for a friend flip to rivalry when she feels left out.

passage: Behind the temple in their small town, the older boy, Gopal, spun his wooden top so it hummed on the dust. Dhruv watched, mouth open. “You're the best! Teach me!” He copied every move, winding the string. When Gopal turned to play with the bigger boys and didn't answer, Dhruv's face fell. He muttered, “You're not even that good.” Usha Dadi, sitting on the step, called him over. “You wanted him to play with you. That feels bad. Let's practise, and tomorrow you show him.”

qa.q: What did Gopal spin?
qa.a: A wooden top.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he muttered “You're not even that good”?
qa.a: He felt left out and hurt when Gopal turned away, so his admiration flipped into rivalry.

qa.q: What did Usha Dadi do to help Dhruv?
qa.a: She named his hurt and offered to practise with him, giving him a hopeful plan instead of sulking.

qa.q: How might Gopal see Dhruv's admiration?
qa.a: He may not have noticed how much Dhruv looked up to him, being busy with the bigger boys.

grounding: A child admires and copies an older boy, then his praise flips to rivalry when he feels left out.

passage: On the kindergarten playground in Lima, Esther watched Alejandro do a cartwheel. “You're amazing! Do another!” She tried one herself and landed on her bottom, laughing. All week she copied him. On Friday, the teacher chose Alejandro to show the class his cartwheel. Esther folded her arms. “He's not even that good. Mine are better.” Alejandro looked confused. Later, the teacher asked Esther to show hers too. Esther did a wobbly one. Alejandro clapped. “You're getting good!” Esther grinned.

qa.q: What did Esther land on when she tried a cartwheel?
qa.a: Her bottom.

qa.q: What was Esther feeling when she folded her arms on Friday?
qa.a: She felt left out and jealous when Alejandro was chosen, so her admiration turned into rivalry.

qa.q: What helped turn the rivalry back into friendship?
qa.a: The teacher gave Esther a turn too, and Alejandro clapped for her, so she felt included.

qa.q: How did Alejandro see Esther's sudden “He's not even that good”?
qa.a: He was confused, since she had been praising him all week.

grounding: A preschooler admires and copies a friend's cartwheels, and her praise flips to rivalry when she feels left out.

passage:
Monday: Divyansh held up his drawing of a train. Disha, scrolling on her phone, said flatly, “Good job.” Divyansh looked at her face, then folded the drawing and put it in the drawer.
Wednesday: He showed her a block tower. Disha put her phone down and smiled. “You used all the long blocks at the bottom so it doesn't wobble!” Divyansh's eyes lit up. “Yes! I thought of that.”
Friday: He brought her three drawings in a row, explaining each one.

qa.q: What did Divyansh draw on Monday?
qa.a: A train.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he folded the drawing and put it away?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and unseen, because the flat “Good job” and her eyes on the phone didn't feel like real interest.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that made the praise land?
qa.a: Disha looked at him, smiled, and said something specific about what he did, the long blocks at the bottom.

qa.q: How might Disha feel on Friday when he brings three drawings?
qa.a: She likely feels happy and a little moved that he now wants to share his work with her.

grounding: Over a week, a child reads flat praise as empty and responds warmly to a smile and specific words.

passage: The power had been out all evening, and Vishal came home after a twelve-hour shift, soaked from the rain. Preeti rushed to him in the candlelight. “Papa, look! I tied my shoelaces myself!” Vishal, dropping onto the sofa, said, “Hmm, good,” without looking. Preeti's smile faded. She sat down slowly. Vishal noticed. He sat up, picked up the candle and looked at her shoes. “Wait, you did a double knot? That's tricky. You made both loops.” Preeti's smile came back. “I practised all day.”

qa.q: What had Preeti done herself?
qa.a: Tied her shoelaces.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when her smile faded?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and let down, because the flat “Hmm, good” without a look felt like he didn't care.

qa.q: What did Vishal do that helped, even though he was exhausted?
qa.a: He noticed her face, looked properly at her shoes, and praised exactly what she did.

qa.q: What would change if Vishal hadn't noticed?
qa.a: Preeti might have gone to bed feeling her effort didn't matter, and stopped showing him things.

grounding: After a long day, a father's flat praise falls flat for his preschooler, and specific words about what she did land better.

passage: In the city school's KG room, Gopika finished a hard jigsaw puzzle. Wasim Sir walked past. “Good job,” he said without stopping. Gopika looked after him. The next day she finished another. This time Wasim Sir knelt beside her, smiled, and said, “You kept trying even when the sky pieces all looked the same. You sorted them by colour first.” Gopika sat up straight. “I did the edges first too.” “Clever plan.” She started another puzzle straight away.

qa.q: What did Gopika sort by colour?
qa.a: The sky pieces.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she looked after Wasim Sir the first day?
qa.a: She probably felt a little disappointed or unsure, since his quick “Good job” didn't show he had really noticed.

qa.q: What made the second praise land better?
qa.a: Wasim Sir knelt, smiled and named exactly what she did, her effort and her colour plan.

qa.q: How might Wasim Sir see Gopika starting another puzzle straight away?
qa.a: He likely feels pleased, seeing that specific praise encouraged her to keep going.

grounding: A preschooler reads praise by tone and attention, and specific words about her effort land better than a passing “Good job.”

subtype: Accepting comfort from a trusted adult [Regulating]
passage: A firecracker exploded in the lane outside the school, so loud the windows rattled. Chetan screamed and dived under the table, shaking. Vikas Sir crouched down and held out his arms. Chetan crawled into them. Vikas didn't say, “Stop crying, it's nothing.” He held him and said quietly, “That was loud. You were scared.” Chetan nodded against his shirt. “Very scared.” “I know. You're safe now.” Slowly Chetan's shaking stopped. He sat on Vikas's lap for the rest of story time.

qa.q: What exploded in the lane?
qa.a: A firecracker.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he dived under the table?
qa.a: He was very frightened by the sudden loud bang, and his shaking showed it.

qa.q: Why was naming the feeling better than saying “Stop crying”?
qa.a: It helped Chetan understand and accept his fear and settle, instead of learning to hide it.

qa.q: What would change if Vikas Sir had said “Stop crying, it's nothing”?
qa.a: Chetan might learn to hide his fear, and he wouldn't have felt safe enough to calm down on his lap.

grounding: A child uses a hug and a lap to settle after a fright, and his teacher names the feeling instead of saying stop crying.

subtype: Accepting comfort from a trusted adult [Regulating]
passage: I'm Bhavna, from the ground floor. This morning a street dog chased Damini at the gate, barking. It didn't touch her, but she ran screaming to her mother and buried her face in her dupatta. Her mother didn't say, “Don't be silly.” She picked her up, sat on the step, and said, “You were scared. The dog ran at you.” Damini sobbed, “It was so loud.” Her mother rocked her. I don't know how long it took, but by the time I came back from the shop, Damini was waving at the dog from her lap.

qa.q: What did Damini bury her face in?
qa.a: Her mother's dupatta.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she ran screaming to her mother?
qa.a: She was frightened by the barking dog, even though it didn't touch her.

qa.q: What did Damini's mother do that helps later self-soothing?
qa.a: She held her and named the feeling, “You were scared,” instead of calling it silly.

qa.q: How did Bhavna see the change in Damini?
qa.a: When Bhavna came back from the shop, Damini was already calm enough to wave at the dog from her mother's lap.

grounding: A neighbour observes a mother comfort her frightened daughter with a lap and by naming the feeling.

subtype: Accepting comfort from a trusted adult [Regulating]
passage:
Monday: Damini woke from a nightmare, crying. Sachin, half asleep, said, “Stop crying, it was just a dream.” Damini pulled the sheet over her head and cried quietly.
Wednesday: Another nightmare. This time Sachin sat on her bed and held her. “You had a bad dream. You were scared.” She nodded. He rubbed her back till she fell asleep.
Saturday: Damini padded into his room. “Papa, I had a scary dream. I was scared.” She climbed up for a hug and was asleep again in minutes.

qa.q: What did Damini do on Monday after Sachin said stop crying?
qa.a: She pulled the sheet over her head and cried quietly.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she hid under the sheet on Monday?
qa.a: She was still frightened, and felt alone and dismissed, so she hid her crying.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: Sachin held her and named her feeling, “You were scared,” which helped her settle.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel on Saturday when Damini names her own fear?
qa.a: He likely feels relieved and proud that she can now say what she feels and settle quickly.

grounding: Over a week, a father learns that naming a child's fear and holding her helps her settle, while stop crying teaches her to hide it.

passage:
Monday: At preschool, Tejas's friend cried after falling. Tejas sat next to him. “Don't cry, I'm here.” He pushed his toy car into his friend's hands. The friend pushed it away and turned his back. Tejas looked hurt.
Wednesday: Irawati Ma'am said, “You were very kind. Sometimes sad people want space. You can ask, ‘Hug, or quiet?’”
Friday: A girl cried at drop-off. Tejas went close and asked, “Hug, or quiet?” She whispered, “Quiet.” Tejas sat a little way off, just nearby.

qa.q: What did Tejas offer his friend on Monday?
qa.a: His toy car.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when his friend pushed the car away?
qa.a: He felt hurt and confused, because his kind offer was turned down.

qa.q: What did Irawati Ma'am teach Tejas?
qa.a: That sad people sometimes want space, and that he can ask “Hug, or quiet?”

qa.q: How might the girl at drop-off feel when Tejas sits nearby quietly?
qa.a: She might feel comforted and respected, having someone near without being crowded.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler's sincere comfort is pushed away, and he learns to ask if a sad person wants help or space.

passage: The power had gone out, and the flat was dark except for a candle. Santosh Dada sat by the window with his phone, waiting to hear from the hospital about Dadi. His eyes were wet. Lokesh came and climbed on the chair beside him. “Don't cry, Dada. I'm here.” He held out his old teddy. “You can have Bholu.” Santosh took the teddy and pulled Lokesh close. “Thank you, beta.” They sat together in the candlelight until the phone buzzed and Dada said, “She's sleeping well.”

qa.q: What was the teddy's name?
qa.a: Bholu.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he climbed up beside Dada?
qa.a: He felt caring and a bit worried, seeing his grandfather's wet eyes.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's comfort work here?
qa.a: Dada wanted closeness, so the teddy and sitting together gave real comfort.

qa.q: What was it like for Santosh Dada to wait with Lokesh beside him?
qa.a: It likely felt less lonely and frightening to wait for news with Lokesh close.

grounding: In a dark, worried evening, a preschooler offers his grandfather a teddy and simple reassurance.

passage: Nitin came home from his cricket match, threw his bat down and went to his room. Uday followed him with a biscuit. “Don't be sad, Bhaiya. Here, I'm here.” Nitin snapped, “Go away, Uday!” Uday's face crumpled. He ran to their mother in the kitchen. She crouched. “You were being very kind. Bhaiya is upset and needs to be alone right now. It's not about you.” Uday sniffed. “Can I give the biscuit later?” “Later is perfect.” An hour later, Nitin ate it gratefully.

qa.q: What did Uday bring to Nitin?
qa.a: A biscuit.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when his face crumpled?
qa.a: He felt hurt and rejected when his kind offer was met with “Go away.”

qa.q: What did their mother explain to Uday?
qa.a: That he was being kind, that Nitin needed to be alone right now, and that it wasn't about him.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt when Uday followed him in?
qa.a: He was upset about the match and wanted space, so Uday's comfort felt like too much at that moment.

grounding: A preschooler sincerely comforts his upset brother, is pushed away, and learns that sometimes people want space.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage: In the lobby of their building, a boy grabbed Akash's ball. Akash's mother, Seema, said, “Please give it back.” The boy muttered, “Sorry,” without looking up, and kept holding the ball. Akash said, “He said sorry,” and turned away, though his lip was shaking. Seema knelt. “He said sorry. Did he give the ball back?” Akash looked. “No.” “A real sorry means you stop and fix it.” She turned to the boy. “Please give it back now.” He did. Akash hugged the ball.

qa.q: What did the boy grab?
qa.a: Akash's ball.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he turned away with his lip shaking?
qa.a: He was upset about his ball and confused, because he accepted the sorry even though nothing changed.

qa.q: What did Seema teach Akash about sorry?
qa.a: That a real sorry means stopping and fixing it, and she helped check whether the ball came back.

qa.q: How might the boy see Seema's second request?
qa.a: He'd learn that saying sorry isn't enough, and that he needed to give the ball back.

grounding: A child accepts a sorry at face value, and his mother helps him check whether repair actually happened.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage:
“Didi, Rohit kicked my chair again.”
“Did you tell him to stop?” asked Sunaina.
“Yes. He said sorry.”
“Did he stop?”
Wasim thought. “No. He kicked it three more times. But he said sorry.”
“Hmm. When someone's really sorry, what do they do?”
“Stop kicking?”
“Yes. How did his sorry sound?”
“Laughy. He wasn't looking at me.”
“So maybe not a real sorry. Tomorrow, if he kicks again, tell your teacher.”
“Okay.” Wasim sighed. “I thought sorry fixed it.”

qa.q: How many more times did Rohit kick the chair after saying sorry?
qa.a: Three more times.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he sighed?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a bit confused, having believed that sorry fixed things.

qa.q: How did Sunaina help Wasim judge the sorry?
qa.a: She asked whether Rohit stopped, how the sorry sounded and whether he looked at him, so Wasim could see it wasn't real.

qa.q: What is it like for Wasim to keep getting kicked after a sorry?
qa.a: It is confusing and frustrating, because the word promised a fix that didn't come.

grounding: A preschooler accepts a sorry at face value, and his sister helps him check tone, eye contact and whether the behaviour stopped.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage:
Note by Vandana, KG teacher.
Today a boy snatched Deepak's crayons. When I stepped in, the boy said “sorry” quickly while looking out of the window, and then grabbed another crayon. Deepak said, “It's okay,” and smiled. I asked Deepak, “Did he stop?” Deepak shook his head. I asked the boy to look at Deepak and give the crayon back. He did, and this time his sorry was quiet and he looked at him. Deepak said, “That one was real.” We'll keep practising what sorry means.

qa.q: Where was the boy looking when he first said sorry?
qa.a: Out of the window.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he said “It's okay” and smiled?
qa.a: He probably felt he should accept any sorry, even though he was upset about his crayons.

qa.q: What did Vandana do to help Deepak check the repair?
qa.a: Vandana asked if the boy had stopped and guided the boy to look at Deepak and give the crayon back.

qa.q: How might the boy feel when asked to look at Deepak and give the crayon back?
qa.a: He may feel a bit embarrassed, but he learns that a real sorry means stopping and giving back.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler accepting any sorry at face value and being helped to check whether repair happened.

passage:
Monday: Ishita pushed a girl off the swing, said, “Sorry!” and ran off to the slide. The girl sat crying on the sand.
Wednesday: Lalremsiami Ma'am sat with Ishita. “When you say sorry, who was hurt?” “Her.” “Where?” Ishita thought. “Her knee.” “How could you help it feel better?” “Bring the ice pack?”
Friday: Ishita bumped a boy in the line. She stopped. “Sorry. Are you hurt?” He rubbed his arm. She fetched the teacher and held his hand while it was checked.

qa.q: What did Ishita do right after saying sorry on Monday?
qa.a: She ran off to the slide.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she said sorry and ran off on Monday?
qa.a: She probably felt a little guilty but wanted the trouble to be over quickly, without understanding the hurt.

qa.q: What questions did Lalremsiami Ma'am use to teach what sorry means?
qa.a: She asked who was hurt, where, and how Ishita could help it feel better.

qa.q: How might the boy feel when Ishita stops and asks if he's hurt?
qa.a: He'd likely feel cared for and less upset, because she noticed and helped.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler moves from a quick sorry to understanding who was hurt and how to help.

passage: The birthday party was packed and noisy, and the cake had just been cut. Divyansh ran past and knocked Gopika's plate out of her hands. Cake splattered on the floor. “Sorry!” he shouted, already running. Gopika's eyes filled. Her aunt caught Divyansh gently by the arm. “Wait. Who was hurt?” Divyansh looked at Gopika. “Her cake fell.” “How does she feel?” “Sad.” “What could fix it?” He thought, then ran to the table and came back carefully with a new slice. “Sorry. Here.”

qa.q: What happened to Gopika's cake?
qa.a: It splattered on the floor.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when her eyes filled?
qa.a: She felt sad and upset that her cake fell, especially when Divyansh just shouted sorry and ran.

qa.q: What did Gopika's aunt do instead of forcing a ritual apology?
qa.a: She stopped Divyansh and asked who was hurt, how she felt and what could fix it, so he understood and repaired it.

qa.q: How might Gopika's aunt see Divyansh's first shouted sorry?
qa.a: She sees it as a quick way to escape, not real understanding, which is why she stopped him to talk.

grounding: At a crowded party, a preschooler says a quick sorry, and an adult helps him learn who was hurt and how to fix it.

passage: In their flat, Hafsa snapped her friend's new pink crayon in half. The friend's face crumpled. Gargi, Hafsa's mother, didn't say, “Say sorry now.” She sat with both girls. “Hafsa, look at her face. How does she feel?” Hafsa looked. “Sad. It was new.” “What could help?” Hafsa thought, then fetched her own pink crayon and held it out. “You can have mine. Sorry I broke it.” Her friend took it and sniffed. “We can share the broken bits.”

qa.q: What colour was the crayon Hafsa broke?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she looked at her friend's face?
qa.a: She probably felt sorry and a bit guilty, seeing her friend was sad about the new crayon.

qa.q: Why was Gargi's approach better than forcing a quick sorry?
qa.a: It helped Hafsa understand who was hurt and find her own way to fix it, so the sorry meant something.

qa.q: How did the friend feel after Hafsa offered her crayon?
qa.a: She felt comforted, and happy enough to suggest sharing the broken bits.

grounding: A mother helps her preschooler understand who was hurt and how to fix it, rather than forcing a ritual sorry.

passage:
Monday: “My tummy hurts,” Uday said at breakfast. Lavanya asked, “Where?” He pointed vaguely. “Everywhere. I don't want the new teacher.” Lavanya hugged him; the ache seemed like worry.
Wednesday: After lunch Uday said, “My tummy hurts, here,” pointing low on one side, and lay down. Lavanya took it seriously and called the doctor to ask.
Friday: Uday was snapping at everyone at dinner. Lavanya asked, “Tummy, hungry or sleepy?” He yawned hugely. “Sleepy.” He was asleep by seven.

qa.q: Where did Uday point on Wednesday?
qa.a: Low on one side of his tummy.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling on Monday when his tummy hurt everywhere?
qa.a: He was probably worried about the new teacher, and the worry showed up as a tummy ache.

qa.q: Why was Lavanya right to call the doctor on Wednesday?
qa.a: The pain was in one place and he lay down, so she took the report seriously instead of assuming it was worry.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's view of Uday's snapping change once he yawns?
qa.a: She sees the snapping as tiredness, not naughtiness, and helps him to bed.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler mixes feelings and body states, and his mother asks where it hurts, takes pain seriously and spots tiredness behind grumpiness.

passage: The bus from the village was stuck behind a broken truck for two hours. Farhan kicked the seat in front. “I hate this bus! I hate everything!” Raghav, his father, was tempted to scold. Instead he asked, “Is it your tummy, are you hungry, or are you sleepy?” Farhan scowled. “Sleepy.” Then, “And hungry.” Raghav found a banana in his bag. Farhan ate it, curled against his arm and was asleep before the bus moved again.

qa.q: How long was the bus stuck?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling behind his “I hate everything”?
qa.a: He was tired and hungry, and those body states came out as anger and grumpiness.

qa.q: Which choice by Raghav worked, and why?
qa.a: He asked simple choices about tummy, hunger or sleepiness, which helped Farhan name his needs, and then met them.

qa.q: What would change if Raghav had scolded Farhan for kicking?
qa.a: Farhan might have cried or kicked more, and his hunger and tiredness would have stayed unmet.

grounding: On a delayed bus, a preschooler's tiredness and hunger show up as irritability, and his father helps him name them.

passage: During drawing time at the city nursery, Lavanya put down her crayon and held her ear. “My ear hurts.” Minakshi Ma'am knelt beside her. “Show me where.” Lavanya touched inside her left ear. “It's going ouch-ouch.” Minakshi didn't say, “You're just tired.” She let Lavanya lie on the cushions and called her mother, who said she'd come and take her to the doctor. Lavanya held Minakshi's hand while they waited. “Is it bad?” “Your mummy's coming, and the doctor will check.”

qa.q: Which ear did Lavanya touch?
qa.a: Her left ear.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling while she waited for her mother?
qa.a: She was worried and uncomfortable because her ear hurt, which is why she asked if it was bad.

qa.q: What did Minakshi Ma'am do that takes a pain report seriously?
qa.a: She asked where it hurt, let Lavanya rest, and called her mother so a doctor could check.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's mother feel getting the call?
qa.a: She'd probably feel concerned but grateful the teacher called straight away.

grounding: A preschooler names an earache at nursery, and her teacher asks where it hurts and takes the report seriously.

subtype: Reading a child's unmet need behind behaviour [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Uma, from next door. At our housewarming, Nitin's daughter Mahi clung to his leg and whined every time he tried to talk to anyone. Nitin didn't snap. He crouched down. “Mahi, is it your tummy, are you sleepy, or is it too noisy?” She said, “Noisy,” and pressed her hands to her ears. He carried her out to the quiet balcony. I don't know if it was only the noise, but after ten minutes she was playing with my cat.

qa.q: Where did Nitin carry Mahi?
qa.a: Out to the quiet balcony.

qa.q: What was Nitin thinking when he crouched and asked Mahi simple choices?
qa.a: He was guessing that something was bothering her, like hunger, tiredness or noise, and wanted her help to be sure, rather than feeling annoyed.

qa.q: What did Nitin's questions help him find out?
qa.a: That Mahi was overwhelmed by the noise, so he could take her somewhere quiet.

qa.q: How did Uma see Mahi's clinginess?
qa.a: Uma wasn't sure it was only the noise, but Mahi did calm down on the balcony.

grounding: A neighbour observes a father read his clingy child's need by offering simple choices at a noisy party.

subtype: Reading a child's unmet need behind behaviour [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: Yamini came home from school cranky and clingy. Jasleen offered a snack; Yamini pushed it away. “Tired?” “No!” Jasleen held her, unsure.
Tuesday: Same again. Jasleen asked, “Is something at school worrying you?” Yamini whispered, “The new class is big. I don't know anyone.”
Thursday: Jasleen had talked to the teacher, who paired Yamini with a buddy. Yamini came home skipping. “Mama, my buddy likes cats too!” She ate her whole snack.

qa.q: What did the teacher do for Yamini?
qa.a: Paired her with a buddy.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling behind her crankiness and clinginess?
qa.a: She was worried and lonely in her big new class where she didn't know anyone.

qa.q: How did Jasleen find the real need?
qa.a: She tried hunger and tiredness, then asked about worry at school, treating her guesses as provisional until Yamini told her.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Jasleen's message?
qa.a: The teacher would likely be glad to know, since a buddy is an easy way to help a worried new child.

grounding: Over a week, a mother tries hunger and tiredness before finding the worry behind her child's crankiness.

subtype: Reading a child's unmet need behind behaviour [Interpreting]
passage: The wedding was loud, the dinner was late, and the photographer wanted the family on stage in five minutes. Rafiq hung on Omkar's arm, whining, rubbing his eyes, then pushing his face into Omkar's shirt. Omkar felt his patience slipping. He crouched. “Food, quiet corner, or my lap?” Rafiq said, “Lap and quiet.” Omkar sat with him behind the stage curtains, where the music was softer. Rafiq's whining stopped almost at once. When they walked on stage for the photo, Rafiq was half asleep on his shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Omkar sit with Rafiq?
qa.a: Behind the stage curtains, where the music was softer.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he crouched to offer choices?
qa.a: He was stressed and his patience was slipping, but he chose to find out what Rafiq needed instead of snapping.

qa.q: Which choice by Omkar worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering simple choices let Rafiq say he needed a lap and quiet, confirming he was tired and overwhelmed by the noise.

qa.q: What would change if Omkar had just told Rafiq to stop whining?
qa.a: The whining would likely have got worse, since his need for rest and quiet wouldn't be met.

grounding: Under time pressure at a loud wedding, a father reads his clingy child's need by offering simple choices.
